title: Sister looks to bring brother's body home
article: A woman from Prince Rupert is hoping people will open their hearts and help her bring the body of her brother home.
"I'm trying to get the message out that we have lost a family member," said Teresa Chenery. "We wanted to ask the community for donations to bring him home for burial."
Gerald Samuel Chenery, 29, was shot and killed by two Vancouver police officers Boxing Day evening in the city's downtown eastside.
"My brother was shot 15 times by police," said Chenery. "I talked with a detective but because it's an investigation, an inquiry I think he said, I guess they can't release any details.
"His body can be released, but we don't have the income \[to bury him\]."

Gerald Chenery remains in the morgue at Vancouver General Hospital while Teresa, his closest living relative, attempts to find a way to have her brother's remains properly looked after. She is on income assistance and supports six children.
"Income assistance said they used to help with bereavement costs, but with all the cutbacks in funding they are no longer under any obligation to help me," she said.
The bother and sister are members of the Lincoln family, but were adopted by an RCMP officer and left Prince Rupert when they were children.
"Gerald was adopted by Sergeant J.W. Chenery," said Teresa Chenery. "Later, he contacted my original family that adopted me, so I could move in with my brother."
The pair lived with the Sergeant for most of their lives in Lillooet.
Teresa had her children there, however Gerald left when he was a teenager.
Although her brother had been in trouble with the law in the past, she is unsure what could have led to the police shooting that claimed his life.
"I talked to my brother on December 23," said Chenery. "He said he was just released from jail and I said 'Good, when are you coming home?'"
He wanted to be reunited with his family, stay out of trouble and help me raise my kids."
The siblings had spoken about land owned by their biological father in Kincolith and the possibility of living in a house together there.
"The last thing he said to me was we'll be together sooner than you think," said Chenery, choking back tears. "Next time I heard about it two police men came to my door (Dec. 27) and took me outside.
"Local RCMP told me my brother was shot to death by Vancouver police and they couldn't give me any information."

What police will reveal is that two officers were conducting a patrol at around 9:30 p.m. Boxing Day when they came upon a man in the south lane of the 200 block of East Hastings Street. A police check revealed Gerald Chenery was wanted on a Canada-wide warrant after his parole had been revoked for failing to report to his halfway house after being released from jail.

When the officers attempted to arrest the man, who had previous offences including those involving a weapon, he pulled a knife on them, said Const. Sarah Bloor, Vancouver police spokesperson. Repeated requests were ignored to drop the knife and he eventually lunged at one of the officers, cutting one of them on the hand, she said.
"It was a regrettable situation in that no officer ever wants to use lethal force," said Bloor. "The officer almost had a knife plunged in her chest.
"\[They\] had to respond."
Police will not reveal the number of times Chenery was shot, except to say they continued to fire as he advanced and that he also drew a second knife.
"There were a number of shots fired as a result of him continuing forward," said Bloor.
Police officers are taught to only use lethal force when they or someone else is in imminent danger of harm, she said.

The officers who shot Gerald Chenery, one male and one female, were on the force for less than a year, causing concerns by some that the rookie cops may have acted improperly. However, the Vancouver Police Department (VPD) is standing by its officers' actions in the unfortunate incident.

"These are fully trained officers that have ... all the capabilities," said Bloor, noting that retirement and transfers have made the VPD a junior department and the pairing of rookie officers a necessary reality.
"The scenarios and simulations are fresh in their minds."
In a smaller detachment, these officers would have also been out on patrol alone, she said.
The officers have received counselling from the Post Critical Incident Trauma Team and will be off work for awhile.

An investigation is being conducted and all evidence, including a civilian eyewitness account, will be turned over to the provincial Crown, who will determine if charges should be pursued against the officers. The coroner's office, in addition to an autopsy and pathology report, will also conduct an inquest. After these processes are complete, police will also investigate their members internally to see if there was a violation of the Police Act.
The Police Complaints Commissioner can then review this process if it is not to everyone's satisfaction.

Teresa Chenery knows these things will take time, after a series of tragedies during the last year. Her brother's death is the fourth she has endured this year including the high-profile death of her niece Kayla Rose McKay, which remains under investigation, a suicide of a nephew and the sudden death of her biological mother from an aneurysm in August.
Now all Chenery wants is to fulfill her brothers last request.
"He wanted to come home," she said. "That was his last wish, to come home."
